metadata.title: Set Counting and Venn Diagram Reasoning
metadata.description: Use two-set identities and Venn regions to find overlaps, only-group counts, unions and neither.
metadata.teachingApproach: Draw the regions; place the overlap; find only-group counts; reconcile all regions with the total.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 4 “Simplification,” printed pages 95–179. Approved scope: Teach the chapter’s two-set identities: n(A−B)+n(A∩B)=n(A), n(B−A)+n(A∩B)=n(B), n(A∪B)=n(A−B)+n(A∩B)+n(B−A), and n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B). Show how to place overlap first in a Venn diagram, then fill the “only A”, “only B”, and outside regions. Cover questions asking how many are in either group, both, only one, neither, or outside the union. Include checking that disjoint regions sum to the total and that an overlap is not double-counted. A learner should translate verbal group data into regions and solve for a missing count.

content.text:
When people can belong to two groups, adding the group totals double-counts those who belong to both. A two-set Venn diagram separates “A only,” “B only,” the overlap, and the people outside both sets so everyone is counted exactly once.

Use a consistent order: place the overlap first; subtract it from each set to find the “only” regions; add the inside regions to find the union; and subtract the union from the full population to find neither.

The main danger in two-set questions is counting someone twice. Think of the diagram as four disjoint regions: A only, A and B, B only, and neither. Since the regions do not overlap, they can be added safely to recover the total.

For sets A and B, put n(A∩B), the number in both, in the overlap first. Then A-only=n(A)−n(A∩B) and B-only=n(B)−n(A∩B). The union means at least one set: n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B). Subtract the overlap once because it was included in both original totals.

If 45 like tea, 36 like coffee, and 18 like both, then tea-only=45−18=27 and coffee-only=36−18=18. At least one=45+36−18=63. The three inside regions 27+18+18 also total 63, which is a useful consistency check.

Draw the regions even if you calculate mentally. It helps separate “both” from “only” and prevents double-counting.

Inclusion-exclusion subtracts the overlap once because it was counted in both n(A) and n(B). If you add the set totals without subtraction, the union will be too large by exactly the overlap count.
In a group of 100, 50 like tea, 42 like coffee, and 20 like both. How many like neither?

inlineData.prompt: In a group of 100, 50 like tea, 42 like coffee, and 20 like both. How many like neither?
hints: Count the union by adding the set totals and subtracting the overlap once.
Subtract that union from the total group of 100.
inlineData.explanation: Union=50+42−20=72. The overlap is subtracted once because it appears in both totals. Neither=100−72=28. Correct option: A.

content.text:
Use inclusion-exclusion to count everyone in at least one set, then subtract from the surveyed total to get neither.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

First solve for the union, then use the total population. These are two separate counts: inside at least one circle, and outside both circles.
Out of 100 people, 52 like music, 40 like dance, and 20 like both. How many like neither?

inlineData.prompt: Out of 100 people, 52 like music, 40 like dance, and 20 like both. How many like neither?
hints: The overlap was counted twice, so subtract it once for the union.
inlineData.explanation: Union=72; neither=100−72=28. Reconstructing the disjoint regions provides a check that the overlap is not counted twice. Correct option: C.

content.text:
Words in the question identify which Venn region is wanted. “Both” means intersection; “either” or “at least one” usually means union; “A only” excludes the overlap; “neither” is outside both circles; “exactly one” adds A-only and B-only but excludes the overlap.

The chapter’s partition identity n(A−B)+n(A∩B)=n(A) says A-only plus both equals all of A. The corresponding rule applies to B. These identities describe the regions separately, while inclusion-exclusion gives the union directly.

For a full group of 80 using the example above, neither=80−63=17. The inside regions plus the outside region must sum to 80; if they do not, revisit the overlap or a subtraction.

Translate the exact wording before choosing a formula. “Only” excludes the overlap; “both” asks for the overlap; “exactly one” adds the two only-regions; “neither” asks for the complement of the union.
45 students like tea and 18 like both tea and coffee. How many like tea only?

inlineData.prompt: 45 students like tea and 18 like both tea and coffee. How many like tea only?
hints: The tea total contains tea-only and the overlap.
inlineData.explanation: Tea-only is the tea total minus everyone in both groups: 45−18=27 students. Correct option: B.

content.text:
“Only” means the overlap is excluded. Subtract the intersection from the total for that set.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

The set total already includes members in both groups. Remove the overlap to isolate the “only” region rather than adding another count.
64 people use the bus and 25 use both bus and train. How many use bus only?

inlineData.prompt: 64 people use the bus and 25 use both bus and train. How many use bus only?
hints: Bus total is bus-only plus both.
inlineData.explanation: Bus-only=64−25=39 people. Reconstructing the disjoint regions provides a check that the overlap is not counted twice. Correct option: D.

content.text:
A missing overlap can be found by rearranging the union formula. If a group has 70 members, 42 joined club A and 38 joined club B, and everyone joined at least one, then the union is 70. So 70=42+38−overlap, giving overlap=10.

Check that the overlap cannot exceed either group total, and that all “only” values remain nonnegative. If every person belongs to at least one set, neither is zero. If the story does not say that everyone joined a set, do not assume the union equals the full population; there may be people outside both circles.

A negative “only” region signals that the figures are inconsistent or that the overlap has been interpreted incorrectly.

A good Venn solution must satisfy the context. Each region should be zero or positive, the overlap cannot be larger than either set, and the full regions should add to the number surveyed.
There are 70 members; 42 joined club A and 38 joined club B. Everyone joined at least one. How many joined both?

inlineData.prompt: There are 70 members; 42 joined club A and 38 joined club B. Everyone joined at least one. How many joined both?
hints: Since everyone is in at least one club, the union is 70.
inlineData.explanation: Everyone is in the union, so 70=42+38−both. Therefore both=42+38−70=10. Correct option: C.

content.text:
Begin with union=first set+second set−intersection. When the question says everyone is counted, set the union equal to the total and rearrange.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

If everyone belongs to at least one set, the outside region is zero and union equals total. Use that condition explicitly instead of assuming it for every problem.
There are 90 people; 55 know French and 48 know Hindi. Everyone knows at least one. How many know both?

inlineData.prompt: There are 90 people; 55 know French and 48 know Hindi. Everyone knows at least one. How many know both?
hints: The overlap equals the sum of set totals minus the union.
inlineData.explanation: Intersection=55+48−90=13. Reconstructing the disjoint regions provides a check that the overlap is not counted twice. Correct option: A.

content.text:
You have completed Set Counting and Venn Diagram Reasoning.

Place the overlap first. Use the union formula to avoid double-counting, subtract the overlap to find “only” regions, and subtract the union from the population to find “neither.” For “exactly one,” add the two only-regions.

Check that all regions are nonnegative and that the disjoint regions sum to the stated population whenever the full total is given.

Sometimes the question asks how many belong to exactly one set. Find A-only and B-only, then add them: exactly one=(n(A)−overlap)+(n(B)−overlap)=n(A)+n(B)−2×overlap.

For 40 in A, 35 in B, and 12 in both, A-only=28 and B-only=23, so exactly one=51. Equivalently, 40+35−2×12=51. The overlap is subtracted twice because none of those people belong to an “only” region.

Finish by adding all the disjoint regions—A-only, both, B-only, and neither if known—and checking that they equal the stated population.

The exactly-one formula subtracts the overlap twice because the overlap should appear in neither of the two only-regions. This is different from the union formula, which subtracts the overlap only once.
46 people joined group A, 31 joined group B, and 9 joined both. How many joined exactly one group?

inlineData.prompt: 46 people joined group A, 31 joined group B, and 9 joined both. How many joined exactly one group?
hints: Find A-only and B-only by removing the overlap from each total.
inlineData.explanation: A-only=46−9=37 and B-only=31−9=22. Exactly one=37+22=59; neither the overlap nor the group totals alone give the answer. Correct option: D.

content.text:
For “exactly one,” do not include the overlap. Subtract it once from each set total, then add the two remaining regions.

Now try a new value set using the same method.

Draw or name A-only and B-only separately before adding them. That makes it clear why the overlap must not be included in the final exactly-one count.
52 use service A, 41 use service B, and 18 use both. How many use exactly one service?

inlineData.prompt: 52 use service A, 41 use service B, and 18 use both. How many use exactly one service?
hints: Remove the overlap from each group total.
inlineData.explanation: A-only=34 and B-only=23, so exactly one=34+23=57. Reconstructing the disjoint regions provides a check that the overlap is not counted twice. Correct option: B.
